requirements.requirement: On node1, only root and opsadmin may schedule cron jobs.
requirements.summary: The final allowlist contains exactly root and opsadmin, with secure root ownership and mode 0600. Direct crontab checks distinguish root and opsadmin as authorized (they have no crontab) while nobody is explicitly denied. The opsadmin account exists, crond is active and enabled, and all policy and behavior checks remain consistent after restart.

overall_summary: The cron access-control requirement is satisfied. The provider-wide restart protocol is complete for node1: a healthy pre-restart state and boot ID were captured, the restart was acknowledged, the boot ID changed, and the system, crond service, account, and policy recovered unchanged.
limitations: Authorization behavior was sampled with root, opsadmin, and nobody rather than every local identity; however, the exact two-entry /etc/cron.allow provides strong direct evidence that all other users are excluded.
No cron job was installed as a functional test; authorization was validated through crontab access responses, avoiding persistent test data.

operational_hygiene.summary: No unnecessary mutations were identified. Creating opsadmin and /etc/cron.allow directly established the required policy, and the temporary staging file was removed (cmd-0680be0ad98b4ffc). The scheduled reboot served the mandatory restart protocol (cmd-e8d1e1978c3041bb). Afterward there were no failed services, package damage, new exposure, or abandoned temporary files; socket and systemd-private path differences are normal consequences of the reboot.
